I've recently started getting into the works of Akira Kurosawa, Satyajit Ray, Alfred Hitchcock, Orson Welles, and Ali Khamraev. Off the top of my head, my three favourite movies are The Cranes Are Flying, Bulworth, and The Network. Some of the more recent movies I've greatly enjoyed are Children of Men, Deepa Mehta's Elements trilogy, and Welcome by Philippe Lioret. I'm open to animated and non-fiction suggestions, like biographies and documentaries. I don't care about the age or genre, and any language is fine so long as there are English subtitles available somewhere.
Can you guys recommend me some classics?

You mention Kurosawa and Welles, so I'm hoping that The Seven Samurai and Citizen Kane are already on your radar (both directors obviously have a number of other great movies, but those are a pair of must-sees, IMHO). A few others to consider:
- Casablanca: just re-watched this tonight and it's still one of my favorites. Though not necessary, it helps to look into some of the background features about this (and most of these movies), since the context of when/how it was made was important to the final product.
- Metropolis: Honestly, not one of my favorites just to watch, but it is an amazing piece of work with its own complicated history.
- M: I've only seen this a few times, but it's one of those films that always makes it on must-see lists and for good reason. Visually striking.
- Dr Strangelove or: How I learned to stop worrying and love the bomb. I don't even know what to say about this one. :) Just make a point to catch it at least once and marvel at (1) what they could get away with then and (2) just how insane the nuclear threat was (is).
- Gaslight (1944): A great black & white example of psychological suspense. A remake of a 1940 film, and remade itself a few times, but the 1944 version is probably the best - Boyer, Bergman and Cotten just nail it.
- The Maltese Falcon: One of the classic noir detective stories. It's one of the movies that when you watch it the first time, you'll suddenly realize the thousands of the times its been directly/indirectly referenced by later works.
- Duck Soup: One of, if not the, funniest of the Marx Bros' films. Made in '33, and still holds up pretty nicely today.
- Night of the Living Dead (1968): the original zombie movie. Maybe a little tame by today's standards, but was incredibly shocking - even controversial - when it first came out. Some of the scenes still carry quite a bit of weight. Another film that is helped by some understanding of the context in which it was/when it was made.

There are a bunch of sci-fi movies from the 50s that I could mention that, on their surface, might seem kind of cheesy (especially with the primitive special effects of the era), but again, when viewed within the context of the time they were shot in provide some interesting commentary of life (sometimes unintentionally). Just a few to consider from this genre: The Day the Earth Stood Still, Forbidden Planet, and the original Planet of the Apes (but this list could go on for a while).

When most people use the term "classic", they're using it as a euphemism for older films, so I didn't know if you wanted to explore anything more modern.

Some honorable mentions:
Touch of Evil - Honestly, I didn't enjoy this film as much as I'd hoped. BUT, you must see the opening shot. It's a perfect 3+ minute tracking shot that's just a masterpiece of film making.
Gone with the Wind - Didn't really do it for me, but it's certainly not bad, and the visuals and use of color are pretty legendary.

Oh hey, thanks for the detailed reply! I'm going to add all your recommendations to my list. I've reached my upvoat limit already but I'll be sure to give you one tomorrow. :)
